item.title: ArrowDB Adds ACID Semantics and Multi-Cloud Storage Support for Vector Databases
item.description:
ArrowDB Adds ACID Semantics and Multi-Cloud Storage Support for Vector Databases

A new update to a high-performance columnar storage engine built on Apache Arrow introduces ACID-like semantics and expanded cloud storage support, targeting vector databases and analytical workloads.

🔍 Overview

The update enhances the storage engine with manifest versioning and conflict resolution to provide ACID-like semantics. It is designed specifically for vector databases and analytical workloads, with a core implementation in C++ and bindings available for multiple languages.

🧩 How it works

The engine organizes columns into groups to optimize I/O and compression. It supports data-at-rest encryption and configurable compression. The primary format is Parquet, with additional support for Vortex and Lance formats.

⚙️ Key details

  • Core Implementation: C++20 compiler required (GCC 10+, Clang 10+, Apple Clang 12+); CMake >= 3.20.0; Conan >= 2.0.
  • Language Bindings:
    • Python: FFI bindings with PyArrow integration.
    • Java/Scala: JNI bindings.
    • Rust: DataFusion TableProvider integration.
    • C++: Primary core.
  • Data Integrity: ACID-like semantics using manifest versioning and conflict resolution.

🚀 Availability

The engine supports major cloud storage providers, including:

  • AWS S3 (including S3-compatible storage such as MinIO, Cloudflare R2, and RustFS)
  • Google Cloud Storage
  • Azure Blob Storage
  • Aliyun OSS
  • Tencent COS
  • Huawei Cloud OBS

#ApacheArrow #VectorDatabases #CloudStorage #CPlusPlus #DataEngineering

Source: milvus-io/milvus-storage

item.title: Goose database migration tool supports Go functions and out-of-order changes
item.description:
Goose database migration tool supports Go functions and out-of-order changes

Goose is a database migration tool available as both a CLI and a library. It allows developers to manage database schemas by creating incremental SQL changes or Go functions.

🔍 Overview

The tool supports migrations for multiple database systems. It works against Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB, Spanner, SQLite, YDB, ClickHouse, MSSQL, and Vertica.

🧩 How it works

Goose supports specific migration formats and operational features:

  • Go migrations written as plain functions.
  • Embedded migrations.
  • Out-of-order migrations.
  • Seeding data.
  • Environment variable substitution in SQL migrations.

⚙️ Key details

The CLI includes flags for configuring migration behavior. The following table details specific flags and their functions:

Flag Description
-allow-missing Applies missing (out-of-order) migrations
-certfile File path to root CA’s certificates in pem format (only supported on MySQL)
-dir Directory with migration files (default “.”, can be set via GOOSE_MIGRATION_DIR)
-env Load environment variables from file (default .env)
-no-color Disable color output (NO_COLOR env variable supported)
-no-versioning Apply migration commands with no versioning, in file order
-s Use sequential numbering for new migrations
-ssl-cert File path to SSL certificates in pem format (only supported on MySQL)
-ssl-key File path to SSL key in pem format (only supported on MySQL)
-table Migrations table name (default “goose_db_version”)
-timeout Maximum allowed duration for queries to run

🚀 Availability

Goose is available via several installation methods:

  • Go Install: go install github.com/pressly/goose/v3/cmd/goose@latest installs the binary to your $GOPATH/bin directory.
  • Homebrew: Available for macOS users.
  • Docker: A container image is available for linux/amd64 and linux/arm64.
    • The container image has no shell and supports .sql migrations only.
    • The working directory is /migrations.
    • Tags include vX.Y.Z, vX.Y, vX, and latest.
    • Dockerfiles can copy the binary using: COPY --from=ghcr.io/pressly/goose:v3.30.1 /usr/local/bin/goose /usr/local/bin/goose

#Goose #Database #Go #CLI #Migrations

Source: pressly/goose

item.title: PostgreSQL 19 Released with New Read-Your-Writes Consistency Feature
item.description:
PostgreSQL 19 Released with New Read-Your-Writes Consistency Feature

PostgreSQL 19 has been released, arriving two months later than the typical September schedule due to a flurry of issues related to AI-reported vulnerabilities.

🔍 Overview

  • The release was delayed from September by two months.
  • The delay was attributed to addressing ongoing AI-reported vulnerability issues.
  • The author considers the release “definitely worth the wait.”

🧩 How it works

The release introduces a “read-your-writes” consistency feature for applications sending reads to standbys using the new WAIT FOR LSN command. This allows a session on a standby to wait until it has replayed the write-ahead log (WAL) up to a specific log sequence number (LSN) before running a query. This ensures the application can read data it just wrote on the primary.

Example Workflow

  1. Update a record on the primary: UPDATE movie SET genre = 'Dramatic' WHERE genre = 'Drama';
  2. Get the current LSN: SELECT pg_current_wal_insert_lsn(); (returns a value like 0/0306EE20).
  3. Store the LSN value (e.g., in a signed cookie).
  4. On a subsequent request, use the stored LSN on a standby: WAIT FOR LSN '0/0306EE20' WITH (TIMEOUT '0.1s');
  5. Run the query: SELECT * FROM movie WHERE genre = 'Drama';

The timeout parameter is optional. If provided, the system returns an error if the replica does not catch up within the specified time.

💡 Why it matters

This pattern ensures users see events in chronological order and maintain a consistent view across subsequent requests. Similar patterns have previously been implemented in hand-rolled solutions:

  • Wikipedia/MediaWiki: Uses a hand-rolled version against MySQL replication, saving the primary binlog position in the session and waiting for replicas to catch up before reads. MediaWiki now uses MySQL’s WAIT_FOR_EXECUTED_GTID_SET() function and falls back to SOURCE_POS_WAIT().

#PostgreSQL #Database #SQL #DataConsistency #WaitForLSN

Source: PostgreSQL 19 Released

item.title: NornicDB combines graph and vector search with sub-millisecond latency
item.description:
NornicDB combines graph and vector search with sub-millisecond latency

🔍 Overview

NornicDB is a distributed, low-latency database that integrates Graph and Vector capabilities with Temporal MVCC. It is designed to provide sub-millisecond performance for HNSW search, graph traversal, and writes.

🧩 How it works

The system allows users to query connected data using Cypher with compatible Bolt drivers. It supports combining graph traversal with vector and full-text retrieval. Historical state can be modeled using MVCC and retained history.

⚙️ Key details

  • Interfaces: Supports Neo4j Bolt/Cypher and qdrant’s gRPC, allowing switching without changes.
  • Features: Includes schemas, managed embeddings, reranking, LLM integration, GPU acceleration, Auto-TLP, Policy-based Memory Decay, and an MCP server.
  • Architecture: Multi-arch support includes CPU, CUDA, Metal, and Vulkan.
  • Integration: Can be embedded in Go applications and supports HTTP interfaces.

🚀 Availability

NornicDB is available via Docker images and native installers.

Platform Instructions
NVIDIA CUDA Use image timothyswt/nornicdb-amd64-cuda-bge:latest
Vulkan Use image timothyswt/nornicdb-amd64-vulkan-bge:latest
macOS Docker does not expose Metal acceleration; native install or local build required for GPU acceleration. Download .pkg installer (arm64 for Apple Silicon, amd64 for Intel) or use Homebrew.
Windows Run .\bin\nornicdb.exe serve

Users can access the admin UI at http://localhost:7474. Benchmark results depend on workload and hardware.

#GraphDatabase #VectorSearch #Cypher #NornicDB #GoLang

Source: orneryd/NornicDB

item.title: Datasette Lite runs full Python web app in browser via WebAssembly
item.description:
Datasette Lite runs full Python web app in browser via WebAssembly

Datasette Lite allows the full server-side Datasette Python web application to run directly inside a user’s browser using WebAssembly and Pyodide.

🧩 How it works

When the demo is launched, the browser downloads and executes a full Python interpreter, installs the datasette package and its dependencies, and starts the application in a Web Worker.

  • Datasette pages are displayed in a full-window <iframe> pointing to URLs under /app/<session>/.
  • A service worker (sw.js) intercepts requests (link clicks, form submissions, fetch calls, static assets) and relays them to the Datasette ASGI application running in Pyodide.
  • This architecture supports Datasette’s own JavaScript, plugin assets, POST forms, CSRF protection, sign-in cookies, and file uploads/downloads.
  • Streaming responses, such as server-sent events or CSV exports, are processed as they are produced.
  • If a client disconnects or aborts a fetch, the Datasette application is notified that the client has disconnected.
  • Cookies are stored in a cookie jar inside the Python ASGI bridge, lasting until the tab is closed or reloaded.

⚙️ Key details

  • Browser Requirements: Requires a browser with service worker support. Private browsing modes that disable service workers are not compatible.
  • Web Worker Support: Requires module workers (Chrome 80, Safari 15, Firefox 114 or later).
  • Python Version: Uses Python 3.14 from Pyodide 314.0.8.
  • Error Handling:
    • 503 returned if the tab has already been closed or reloaded.
    • 504 returned if the tab stops answering partway through a request (after four minutes).
    • 500 returned if the Pyodide worker itself fails.
    • 409 returned if a tab was opened before an incompatible update.
  • Session Management: Each tab receives a random session identifier, allowing multiple instances with different data to run simultaneously.
  • Navigation: The page mirrors the iframe’s location into its fragment to ensure the back button works and URLs are bookmarkable.
  • Security: Links to external sites open in a new window with noopener.

🚀 Availability and Versioning

Datasette Lite uses the most recent Datasette release from PyPI by default, including alpha and beta previews.

  • Stable Release: Append ?ref=stable to the URL.
  • Specific Release: Pass a version number as ?ref=.
  • Preview Release: ?ref=pre is equivalent to leaving ?ref out.
  • Source Code: Other ?ref values are treated as branches, tags, or commits in the simonw/datasette GitHub repository.
    • Example: https://lite.datasette.io/?ref=main runs the latest development code.
    • Short SHAs made up only of digits are read as version numbers; full 40-character SHAs are required for specific commits.
    • ?ref values that look like version numbers are always installed from PyPI.
  • Plugin Installation: ?install= works for plugins, requiring a commit with a pyproject.toml.
  • CORS Handling: GitHub source zip files are downloaded through a Cloudflare Worker to add necessary CORS headers.

#Datasette #WebAssembly #Pyodide #SQLite #Python

Source: simonw/datasette-lite
